The half-yearly exams at the Nagaur government school started at nine, and the exam centre this year was across town. In the last exams, Chaitanya had reached the gate and found his admit card still on his desk at home. His friend Rafiq's father had driven him back, and he had lost half an hour of writing time.

Admit card. School ID. Two pens, one spare. Pencil and eraser. Geometry box. Water bottle.
He laid each thing on the bed and put it into a plastic folder, ticking as he went. Then he folded the list and kept it inside the folder too.
In the morning, Rafiq knocked. "Got everything?"
Chaitanya held up the folder. "Checked last night. List is inside."
He used the same list, every night, for all six papers.

I'm Seema, and I work with Uma in the biochemistry teaching lab. She's the lab assistant for the second-year practicals, and I've watched her do the same setup forty times now.
There's a laminated card taped by the fume hood. Twelve steps, in order: gloves, check the balance is zeroed, label the tubes, prepare buffer, warm the water bath, and so on.
Uma knows these steps by heart. But every single time, she runs her finger down the card and says each step softly under her breath. Even at eight in the morning, when she's clearly exhausted.
Last Thursday, the students were already walking in and she was rushing. Her finger stopped at step six. "Water bath," she said. It was still off. She switched it on and waited ten minutes.
The experiment would have failed without it. I don't think she even looked stressed. She just followed the card.

qa.a: Twelve steps, in order.

qa.a: It suggests she feels calm and careful, trusting the card even when she is tired or rushed, though Seema can only guess.

qa.a: She could add a line for the time each step needs, like the water bath's ten minutes, so rushing mornings are planned better.

Dear Akash,
You asked me to write down what went wrong at the Sonepat plant, so you can share it with the new technicians. Here it is, honestly.
On the 14th, I did the monthly check on the new packing machine. I used the same checklist we use for the old ones: belts, oil level, sensors, emergency stop, guard doors. Every line was fine. I ticked all twenty and signed.
What I didn't think about was that this new model has a heating unit for sealing. The old ones don't. Nothing on the list mentions heat. The seal bar was running too hot, and I never looked.
Two days later it scorched a batch and the line stopped for six hours.
The list made me feel I had checked everything, when I had only checked the old machine's problems.
Please tell the team: a new machine needs new questions.
Siddharth

We'd just got a new digital machine. I was the technician on duty. I had the old daily checklist, twenty lines, and I'd done it maybe three hundred times. Power, cooling fan, cables, lead aprons, door warning light. Tick, tick, tick. Signed at 8.05.

Thursday. In the review, Ojas put the checklist on the screen. "We add one line: send release notes to the client's support lead a day before." Tanuja raised her hand. "And these two lines, 'restart the old server' and 'copy files to the backup drive'? We haven't had either of those since we moved to the cloud." They crossed both out.
Two weeks later. The next release went out with a checklist one line shorter than before. The client's support lead replied to the notes the day before: "Thanks, we're ready."

Hemant, you've got a checklist on your desk that's three pages long, and you don't read half of it. Let your Zainab Khala tell you what we did at the bank branch when I was about your age.
We had a checklist for opening the vault in the morning. One day a new cashier forgot to log the second key holder's name. The auditor caught it. A big fuss.
Our manager called us together. She didn't shout. She said, "Let's fix the list, not the person." We added one line: second key holder signs here. Then she asked, "Which lines do we skip because they don't matter anymore?" There were two: checking the old alarm panel, which had been replaced, and ringing the regional office, which we now emailed. Out they went.
After every incident after that, we did the same. Add what we missed. Remove what's dead. The list stayed one page for eleven years, beta.

I'm Dhruv, and Mridul is my neighbour. Every evening his mother used to shout, "Mridul, shoes!" because he kicked them off in the doorway and ran inside.
Last month something changed. I was at his house after school, and he took off his shoes in the doorway like always. But then he stopped, looked at them, and said to himself, "Shoes by the door, then rack." He picked them up and put them on the wooden rack.
I asked why he talked to his shoes. He said, "If I see them there, I put them away. That's the rule. Then I don't have to remember."
Now I notice it every day. He sees the shoes, and his hands just do it. His mother hasn't shouted about shoes all month. I don't know if he's proud, but he grins a little every time.

Monday. Tenzin came home from school, dropped his shoes in the doorway, and his older sister Binita tripped over them carrying the laundry. "Every single day!" she said.
That night Tenzin lay in bed thinking. He always forgot because he was thinking about snacks, not shoes. So he needed something to remind him that wasn't his memory.
Tuesday. He made a rule and said it out loud at the door: "If I see my shoes on the floor, then they go on the rack." He put them there. It felt silly.
Wednesday. He came in, saw the shoes, and his hands moved before he thought about it. Rack.
Two weeks later, Binita came home and stopped. There were no shoes in the doorway at all. "Did Amma make you do this?"
"No," Tenzin said, eating his biscuit. "The shoes remind me."

Dear Lokesh,
You asked how I handle the gang at the back gate who bunk the last period. Here's my secret, and it's not bravery.
Last month they asked me to come to the arcade with them during Hindi. I stood there with my mouth open, didn't know what to say, and nearly went, just because saying no felt awkward.
That night I thought about it. The problem wasn't that I wanted to go. It was that I had no words ready. So I decided: if they ask me to skip class, then I say, "I've got a test, catch you after," and walk to class. Same words every time. No explaining.
Yesterday they asked again. I said it without even thinking and walked off. Nobody even argued.
Try it. Pick your line before they ask.
Baljeet

In Class 11 my friends started skipping the Saturday practical and going to the lake. They'd ask right outside the lab, with everyone watching. The first two times I made up long excuses and they laughed. The third time I just went. And I hated it the whole afternoon.

Bhupen's hostel room in the Tezpur college was always noisy in the evenings, and his flashcards for the English entrance test sat in a rubber band on the shelf, untouched. Every night he promised himself he'd do them. Every night he didn't.
His senior Naveen said, "You brush your teeth every morning without fail, right?"
"Obviously."
"Then tie the cards to that. After brushing, five cards. Nothing else."
The next morning Bhupen brushed his teeth at the corridor sink, came back, and picked up five cards from the stack by his toothbrush mug. Five words. Two minutes.
By the end of the month, the rubber band had moved to a second stack: words he knew. He hadn't missed a single morning, because he hadn't missed a single brushing.

qa.a: Five cards.

qa.q: How had Bhupen been feeling about the untouched flashcards?
qa.a: He was probably guilty and frustrated, promising himself every night and never doing them.

qa.a: Because brushing already happens every morning without fail, so it reminds him automatically, while the noisy evenings kept pushing the cards aside.

qa.q: How does Naveen's suggestion look to Bhupen at first?
qa.a: It seems almost too simple at first, but it gives Bhupen a small habit he actually keeps.

Xin suggested something she'd read about. "Don't find new time. Hook it to something you already do."
"Like what?"
"You brush your teeth every day. After that, five cards."
So he put the flashcard box beside the sink. Every morning, toothbrush back in the cup, then five cards, reading each one aloud while the kettle boiled.
After three weeks, he'd gone through the whole box once. He told Xin, "I never had to remember. The toothbrush remembers for me."

If the supply order is late, then call the vendor before ten. If a doctor asks for a meeting, then offer Tuesday or Thursday. If... Thirty-eight rules in all.
On Wednesday, everything happened at once. Two staff called in sick, the pharmacy delivery didn't come, and a senior doctor wanted a meeting right now.
Baljeet, her assistant, found her at the desk flipping through the four pages. "Which rule is this?"
"I don't know," she said. "I can't find anything."
By noon she had stopped looking at the pages altogether. She was just answering whoever was loudest, the same as last month.

If a new request comes in, then ask for the deadline before saying yes.
If a meeting has no agenda, then ask for one.

Vidya stopped and looked at it. "Walk slow," she said out loud. "Both hands. Then on the table."

"Thank you, Vidya," Ma'am said. "You planned it first, didn't you?"
Vidya nodded and smiled.

subtype: Approach: imagines the steps before acting, sometimes out loud [Thinking]
passage:
I'm Harsha, Hafsa's cousin. Last Sunday Hafsa's Ammi asked her to take a glass of milk to her Abbu.
Hafsa picked it up, then stopped in the kitchen doorway. She whispered to herself, "Slow feet. Both hands. Put on the table." She said it twice, like a song.
Then she walked. Very slowly. Her eyes never left the milk. When the cat ran past, she froze, waited, and then kept going.
She put it on the table with both hands, very carefully. Her Abbu said, "Shabash!"
I don't know exactly what was in her head. But she seemed to be picturing the walk before she took it.

qa.q: What did Hafsa's Abbu say when she put the glass down?
qa.a: Her Abbu said, "Shabash!"

qa.q: What might Hafsa's whispering to herself suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was a little nervous about spilling and was calming herself by picturing each step, though Harsha can't be sure.

qa.q: What could help Hafsa if the cat runs past again?
qa.a: Stopping and waiting, as she did, is a good choice; she could also add "stop if something moves" to her little song.

qa.q: How might Hafsa's Abbu feel when she brings the milk?
qa.a: He feels proud and pleased, which is why he says "Shabash!"

grounding: It shows a young girl saying the steps to herself before carrying a glass, picturing the walk to avoid a spill.
